text: Every form in ServiceNow — an Incident, a Change Request, a custom record — has a Configure menu on the header with a Form Layout option. Opening it shows two columns: on one side, every field that exists on this table but isn't currently on the form; on the other, the fields currently shown, in the order they appear. You move fields across with the arrow buttons, drag to reorder the shown side, and save. Nothing here creates or deletes a field. You're only changing which fields this particular form displays, and in what order — a view-level decision, not a schema change.

A long form like Incident doesn't show forty fields in one unbroken column. It's broken into sections — labeled groups of fields, often rendered as tabs like Notes, Closure Information, or SLA. Sections exist purely for usability. A caller doesn't need to see closure-code fields until the incident is actually being resolved, so those fields live in a section that's easy to collapse or ignore until needed. Form Layout lets you add a new section, assign fields to it, and reorder sections the same way you reorder individual fields.

Hiding a field permanently works when it should never appear on a table. But often the need is conditional — mandatory only when Category is Hardware, hidden unless the caller is a VIP. That's what a UI Policy is for: a record, configured through System UI, that says when a condition is true, make fields visible or hidden, mandatory or optional, read-only or editable. UI Policies run live in the browser as the user fills out the form. This course only introduces the concept — the underlying scripting comes later in this path.

It's tempting to think removing a field from a form deletes it, but that's not what happens. The field's actual definition — name, type, length, default — lives in sys_dictionary, exactly as Chapter 3 covered. Form Layout only controls whether this one form displays that field. The data is still there on every record, and other forms, reports, and lists on the same table can still reference it. Knowing the difference between hiding a field and deleting it separates a careful admin from one who causes avoidable panic.

Form Layout moves and groups fields that already exist. UI Policies add conditional behavior on top of that layout. And underneath both, the table dictionary stays the single source of truth for what a field actually is. Keep those three ideas separate and form configuration stops feeling mysterious.
You've seen how forms are laid out and conditionally controlled. Next up: configuring what a list view actually shows, in what order, and how a table can have more than one named view at once.
